title: Generative methods
thesis: A generator is encoded design knowledge, not free content: its worth lies in how its output is shaped, checked and selected, not in how much it can produce. Pick methods by the experience you want, from weighted lists and grammars to noise, wave function collapse, constraint solvers and language models; then make the output perceptibly different, provably playable and visible to you through sampling, metrics and simulated players. Keep a human — designer, curator or player — in the loop wherever quality matters.

sections.heading: Deciding to generate: what procgen is for
sections.brief: Open with the question Isaac Karth poses: why do you want to generate this, and what should it do to the player? Set Alexei Pepers' warning that procgen is powerful but unpredictable magic, not a fix for every problem, beside Bruno Dias's claim that generation must be integral to the design and Darius Kazemi's point that a game's rules are the context that makes generated content meaningful. Stage the visibility problem: Gabriel Koenig's observation that a once-played game's generation is indistinguishable from handmade content, and that Jettomero's behind-the-scenes systems added almost nothing. Then lower the barrier: Xalavier Nelson Jr.'s 'picking from lists is procgen' and modular pieces, Martin Pichlmair's plea for simple generators, Todd Furmanski's history (memory savings then, scale now), and Brian Walker's reminder that procedural level design is a different, not easier, skill. End with Gillian Smith's guidance to choose a generative system as a material, by the experience you want.

sections.heading: What a generator is: possibility space, cost and encoded knowledge
sections.brief: Give the reader the vocabulary the rest of the chapter uses. Start with possibility space versus generative space (Oliver Withington) and Gillian Smith's framing of procgen as designing an acceptable space of experiences, then Everest Pipkin's view that building a generator is curatorial work that finds the edges of an interesting space. Younès Rabii's thermodynamic formalism carries the middle: seed-to-artifact functions, Kolmogorov complexity, temperature, the solid/liquid/gaseous states, and his central claim that a generator's minimum information volume is the designer knowledge it encodes, so generation is never free and its sorting depends on hidden human labour. Add Cole Wehrle's unseen possibilities and imagined impossibilities and Paul Hembree's note that a slightly finer resolution can explode a learnable space. End with the practical consequence: budget for the knowledge you must encode, and know which space you are tuning.

sections.heading: The oatmeal problem: variety players can actually perceive
sections.brief: Argue that uniqueness is not interest. Converge Darius Kazemi, Kate Compton's '10,000 bowls of oatmeal' (via Isaac Karth, Pierre Vigier, Todd Furmanski and Ada Null), Cole Wehrle's 'one frame of static', Sonat Uzun's similar-sounding Tea Garden songs and Rabii's claim that scale without knowledge drifts toward white noise; this convergence is the section's backbone. Then the positive theory: Nat Alison's order-versus-chaos and surprise, Ada Null's deliberate aim at perceptual differentiation short of uniqueness, Tyler Coleman's point that players talk about outliers so rare weird combinations must be possible. Give the techniques: Kazemi's layered small decisions, Furmanski's multiplied independent categories, and Karth's diagnostic lenses (invariants, repetition and 'mushroom' background content, style, framing, Elite Dangerous's identical docking ports). Close on Linas Gabrielaitis's critique of 'infinite' worlds and practical guidance for designing for memorable difference.

sections.heading: Shaping randomness: distributions, weights and causal structure
sections.brief: Lead with Herbert Wolverson: in good procedural games randomness feeds an algorithm that approximates what the designer wants. Then the toolkit for non-uniform randomness: Tyler Coleman's 'never roll alone' and easing curves, Nifflas's desire bars that raise the odds of overdue events, human-invented and crowd-voted number sequences, Jurie Horneman's weighted multi-metric scoring, and Todd Furmanski's indexed noise tables that ramp difficulty. Alex Byaly's causal graphs get a full subsection (roll the cause, adjust the effect's raffle tickets, roll order, runaway quirks). Use Terry Riley's In C (Matt Carney) and Sonat Uzun's hand-written song structures as models of fixed structure with free variation and a designed ending, and close with Shawn Main's observation that removing either kind of randomness turns a roguelike into a puzzle game.

sections.heading: Seeds, hashes and timing: when content comes into being
sections.brief: Two linked decisions: how randomness is sourced and when generation happens. First, Andrew Clifton's 'don't generate, hash' (what the hash must include, SplitMix64 streams, stateless indexed randomness, tolerable modulo bias), converging with Alexander Birke's Sea of Rifts, which uses hash/noise functions for thread safety and determinism, layers one generator per aspect off a master seed, and insists determinism is needed to reproduce player bugs; bleeptrack's NFC-tag seeds are a light example. Second, timing: the lightning talk's spectrum from Dwarf Fortress world history to generating at first interaction, Birke's per-cell generation on entry (and why WFC does not suit it), Mark Johnson's lazy generation that keeps abstract descriptions of unbuilt places so clues stay true, Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans' game-master-style just-in-time reseeding, and Max Kreminski's mining (space, on demand) versus gardening (time, on a clock). End with guidance on choosing a seeding scheme and a generation moment.

sections.heading: Building blocks for terrain and space: noise, cells, distance and geometry
sections.brief: A technical section, specific enough to implement from. Cover Perlin/Simplex noise and its parameters plus Wolverson's zoom-dependent second layer, Voronoi with distance metrics, and Dijkstra maps as the workhorse for map checks. Cellular automata: Ian Holmes's broad definition, Scott Anderson's Margolus neighbourhood, Greg L's bit-packed Life and row-at-a-time flood fill, Josh Galecki's single-open-neighbour maze. Loren Schmidt's inverse terrain solver is the case study (start from a land/water bitmap, walk uphill from shores, noisy steps, per-terrain wave-front speeds, voting rules, lake detection, region-wise CA rules, hybrid hand-made maps) and should be set against the warnings that noise handles terrain transitions badly and physical simulation (Schmidt, bleeptrack) gives poor direct control. Finish with Adrian Herbez's procedural meshes for 3D printing as the geometric case.

sections.heading: Generating from examples: wave function collapse and its relatives
sections.brief: Explain wave function collapse (WFC) from first principles using Brian Bucklew's pile-of-cards intuition and Adam Newgas's solver framing (overlapped versus tiled, AC3 propagation, model synthesis as its ancestor), then show why it matters: one routine plus tiny paint-program inputs replacing many bespoke algorithms in Caves of Qud. Give the practical controls (interior colours, multi-cell tiles for hand-made pieces, painted edge types, inpainting around fixed tiles, region-driven weights, Townscaper's no-randomness variant, Sergio Garces's Carcassonne framing), then the limits that several talks converge on: homogeneous, locally similar output, overfitting detailed inputs, memory cost, contradictions, and the Qud fix of wrapping WFC in higher-level structure. Set Emily Halina's critique (local patterns miss global key-and-door constraints) against WFC and present her tree-based reconstructive partitioning (TRP), which derives a level skeleton from an MCTS agent's playthrough, with its plagiarism-versus-chaos segment trade-off. End with when to reach for example-based generation versus constructive generation.

sections.heading: Describe the result, not the steps: constraint solving and search
sections.brief: Argue Adam Newgas's thesis that constraint-based generation lets you describe what output should be like instead of how to build it, supported by Pierre Vigier (constraints are intuitive and give guarantees) and Kate Compton (off-the-shelf solvers like answer set programming, and the cost of hand-rolled generate-and-discard). Walk through implementation: Vigier's room-furnishing CSP, randomised backtracking and efficient constraint checks; Knotwords' backtracking fill; Dead Cells' brute-force room fitting at thousands of tries per level; droqen's Sudoku-poem search with most-constrained-first ordering and cheap rejection. Then the costs: more constraints mean more contradictions (Newgas), content constraints remove the designer's usual fixes and make valid outputs rare (droqen), and global properties like symmetry resist local rules (Ian Holmes). Include Karth's point that a generator constrained to compatible elements always yields something usable, and Emoji Economy's runtime optimisation as a non-spatial use.

sections.heading: Guaranteeing the output works: solvability, validation and failure
sections.brief: Start with the rule several talks converge on: guide your randomness, then check the result (Herbert Wolverson), because a shipped generator must be good essentially every time (deepnight) and computers cannot judge human difficulty unaided (Jack Schlesinger). Brian Walker's line between tolerable edge cases and progress-blocking failures sets the standard. Present the strategies: generate-and-test in randomizers (Stella Mazeika) and Ben Berman's MCMC framing of heuristic generators; Josh Galecki's analytic versus constructive solvability with Moondrop's Lights Out proof and dam puzzle; starting from a solution (Galecki, Good Sudoku's symmetric removal); solvers that also power hints; Knotwords' keep-and-regenerate refinement. Then failure stories: Moondrop's silently unsolvable maze and Star Trek (1971)'s regenerate-versus-overwrite bugs. Set the counterweights against all this: Alexei Pepers' account that Caves of Qud keeps generators unconstrained until harm is proven, and Bjarke Alexander Larsen's point that unchecked randomness is fine if players can handle bad outcomes.

sections.heading: Grammars and corpora: generating text and structure from rules
sections.brief: Begin with Bruno Dias's Voyageur (human-written sentence chunks expanded by a Tracery-like grammar, filtered against an evolving model of the planet) and Kate Compton's Tracery, then Abdelrahman Madkour's formal definition of grammars as rewriting and his warning that rules map unintuitively to outputs. Extend to graph grammars (Madkour; Mark Gritter's Emoji Economy) and the strength several talks note: they preserve structural invariants, as in Joris Dormans' Unexplored. Cover corpus-driven text: Jason Grinblat's Markov chains (order, prefix frequency, hooks and the formula for tuning embedded secrets) and his claim that the corpus is what makes it interesting, converging with Everest Pipkin on rules layered over corpora. Practical text machinery: Kingdom of Loathing's word buckets, mad-lib grammar handling, per-generation state and deliberately rare recursive absurdity; Sraëka-Lillian's phonology-based names; Clarissa Littler's poetry generator family, wave and signal functions, grab-bag rhymes, and her warning about stacked constraints.

sections.heading: Generating rules, histories and stories
sections.brief: Lead with Mike Cook's case that roguelikes should generate rules and mechanics, not just levels, then his ladder of approaches: rearranging modular options (Invisible, Inc., Slay the Spire dailies), design languages (Noita wands, Baba Is You, Qud mods) that must make absurd statements hard to write, direct code generation, and filtering generated mechanics with constructed test scenarios. Then histories: Jason Grinblat's retroactive causation in Caves of Qud (pick an event, rationalise a cause) and Bjarke Alexander Larsen's simulated-then-corrupted databases. Then stories: Stephen G. Ware's story planners (events with preconditions, classical versus story planning, runtime limits and heuristics, the too-broad/too-narrow definition problem, LLMs' weak long-term planning) and Max Kreminski's story sifting in Felt, with the difficulty of hand-authoring sifters and Synthesifter's inductive synthesis from examples. Close with Jasmine Otto's 'converse with the deck' retelling test as a way to check a story generator.

sections.heading: Seeing what your generator makes: sampling, metrics and expressive range
sections.brief: Start from Withington's and Madkour's admission that evaluating a generator is hard and open, and from content sampling as the universal but misleading first step. Present expressive range analysis as the field's converging answer (Madkour, Withington, the 2018 lightning talk, Kate Compton's expressive space tools, Mike Cook's Danesh), stressing that metrics are game-specific proxies, not quality functions, and adding dimensionality reduction, guided sampling of outliers and clusters, ERA as pseudo bug-finding, and Emily Halina's fair-comparison rules. Set Karth's snowflake-versus-blizzard lenses and Mike Cook's city/street/lens method (judge a generator by its collisions with other systems, field-survey one location, crop one screenshot, ration your exposures, Liam Wong's Night City) against purely statistical evaluation. Include Mark Gritter's exhaustive enumeration of Rogue's 32-bit seed space and Elliot Trinidad's read-ten-aloud ratio checks. End with a layered evaluation routine: sample, plot, inspect extremes, then look in context.

sections.heading: Steering a generator: parameters, optimisation and learning from examples
sections.brief: Once you can see the generative space, you need levers to move it. Start with Madkour's principle that parameterising a generator turns its expressive range into something steerable, and Aaron Santos's diagnosis of undocumented, interacting magic numbers. Present the two automated routes and set them against each other: Santos's loss functions and mini-batch gradient descent (pull out magic numbers, pass randomness in, the loss as documentation of intent; differentiable versus genetic approaches), versus Madkour's warning that hill climbing and genetic search hide control from the designer, and his learning-from-examples alternative that reweights a graph grammar toward outputs the designer selects, with its limit that reweighting cannot add diversity. Close with lighter levers: Halina's point that an instant generator makes guess-and-check tuning viable, and Sonat Uzun's control by editing the contents of a pool.

sections.heading: Simulated players: solvers, Monte Carlo and tree search as evaluators
sections.brief: Argue that a model of the player is the strongest evaluator a generator can have. Jack Schlesinger's 'your puzzle is a secret dungeon' leads: solving techniques as monsters and the solve order as a path, solver rules derived from play and playtests, difficulty scored per technique with beginner and expert solvers, interestingness read from the solver's path, and variance across runs to reject order-dependent puzzles; droqen's use of an off-the-shelf solver to grade strategies converges. Then Phenry Ewing's Monte Carlo simulation for balancing, with its warnings about model accuracy, representative sampling and realistic weights. Then Lachlan Kingsford's Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS: UCB explained, the four-step loop, chance nodes, reward shaping for long games like NetHack) chosen because it is understandable, set against Emily Halina's note that MCTS-driven generators need a reward function and forward model. End with Ezra Szanton's suggestion to mine real-player analytics for synergy networks.

sections.heading: Generators a team can work with: languages, pipelines and debugging
sections.brief: Shift from algorithms to the environment around them. Lead with Spencer Egart's node-based tools that expose a generator to non-engineers (with branching pipelines) and Kate Compton's 'Compton completeness' test, then her 2020 criteria that a generative language is its whole environment and should be scaffolded, unfoldable and little, plus her earlier point that plain-text data lets users bend a generator to new purposes. Add Liza Knipscher's single unified generator for every living thing in Bioloom as an architectural simplification. Then debugging and workflow: Patrick Kemp's warning that procedural configs can silently generate bad content and his wish for a statistics dashboard, Compton's visualisation of content coverage, Mark Johnson's generate-in-isolation-thousands-of-times routine, and Ada Null's example-first method of hand-writing the desired output before building the generator.

sections.heading: Humans in the loop: curation, collaboration and responsibility
sections.brief: Argue that most good generated content has a human selecting it. Converge Ben Berman (influential generated content relies on curation), Emilia Lazer-Walker (real-time generators cannot curate), Martin Pichlmair (rules plus randomness plus a human activity of selection, as in cut-ups) and Botnik's word-by-word instrument; Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans auto-mutation shows quality collapse when player selection is removed, which leads into players as collaborators and owners of generation (Koenig, Jettomero's photo mode). Then the designer's relationship to the generator: Pepers' arcane/divine/bard/sorcerer mindsets and bonsai pruning, Atty Vohra's 'yes, and' partner, Uzun's happy accidents. Set Nat Alison's defence of hand-crafted Sudoku (solver-assisted grids still feel procedural; using solvers well; hand-crafted versus procedural as a spectrum of intent; design as discovery) against the generator-first views. End on Pepers' warning that algorithms are not neutral and do not absolve their makers.

sections.heading: Machine learning and large language models
sections.brief: Two strands, in this order. First, learning levels from data: Ben Berman's trade-off between data hunger and designer specification, the char-RNN Mario levels, encoding tricks (snaking read order, semantic categories, denoising as an image), ripping training data from mods and his warning about buggy public code, set against Emily Halina's point that games rarely have enough data and the warnings that ML output can look right but not function and leaks uncleaned training data. Second, internet-trained generators: Janelle Shane's Baltimore Orioles effect, context leakage and bias, prompt injection, and her advice to decide early and to generate and hand-pick ahead of time rather than expose the model to players; Robin Sloan's GPT-2 practice (fine-tuning, sentence-count prompts, accumulating context, sharp turns, hidden prompts, never piping raw output to readers, veto-and-regenerate) and his demand that a generator earn its place; Hidden Door's containment of LLM chaos within rules and its preference for ranking and embeddings. End with Gillian Smith's call for the procgen community to lead the public conversation about AI.

sections.heading: Found structures: real-world data, mathematics and the other arts
sections.brief: The chapter's frontier: generators built from borrowed material. Lead with Tyler Coleman's data bending and his method for data-driven generation (understand the shape of input and output, what the player needs, keep the source's flavour), then his warnings about cherry-picking and his point that who chooses the data shifts creative labour. Converge with other real-world inputs: Max Hawkins's map-sample-commit randomizer and its noisy corpus, Neutrinowatch's news and planetary inputs, Younès Rabii's bit-flipped Pokemon ROM. Then mathematics: Paul Hembree's found mathematical objects and Bjorklund's algorithm, Nat Alison's case for studying the model itself, the chaos-theory mirror image. Then the other arts: Mark Gritter's Sol LeWitt and serial art (commit to all consequences of an algorithm), Matt Carney's endogenous/exogenous distinction, and Linas Gabrielaitis's geological folding as an open idea for layered levels.
